# Graphs next to vectors

Graph retrieval, often called **GraphRAG**, adds a graph of entities to vector search. A query first
takes the chunks whose embeddings lie closest to the question, then follows the graph from those
chunks to others that mention the same entities, and passes both sets to the model as context.
Postgres can hold the graph in two ordinary tables next to the `vector` column and walk it with a
join or a recursive query. On the lab's doc-search corpus, the walk added context that the five
nearest chunks missed, but taking the next five nearest chunks added more.

## The graph tables

An entity is a named thing that the text talks about, and a mention links an entity to a chunk
that names it. Chunks and entities together form a bipartite graph, in which a step from a chunk
always leads to an entity and a step from an entity always leads back to a chunk:

```sql
CREATE TABLE doc_entities (id serial PRIMARY KEY, name text UNIQUE NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE doc_mentions (
    chunk_id int REFERENCES doc_chunks (id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    entity_id int REFERENCES doc_entities (id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    PRIMARY KEY (chunk_id, entity_id)
);
CREATE INDEX ON doc_mentions (entity_id);
```

The primary key serves the step from a chunk to its entities, and the index on `entity_id` serves
the step back. GraphRAG libraries usually ask an LLM to extract entities and relations from each
chunk. The SQLAlchemy documentation behind the lab's [doc-search app](pgvector.qmd#the-doc-search-app)
needs no model, because its reStructuredText source marks every API name with a role such as
``:class:`.Session` `` or ``:meth:`.Session.commit` ``. The
[graph notebook](../notebooks/graph_rag_playground.ipynb) reads these roles while it re-chunks the
pages exactly as the ingest did, and finds 440 entities with 1,436 mentions across the 407 chunks.
Only 33 chunks mention no API name.

## Hops and hubs

A few entities appear in a large share of the chunks. `Session` is mentioned in 104 of the 407,
`Table` in 53 and `Engine` in 44, while 242 entities appear in a single chunk and connect nothing.
Through the hubs, an average chunk lies two hops from 61 others, and from 11 once the nine entities
that appear in more than 20 chunks are left out.

A recursive CTE walks the graph to any depth. Starting from a chunk of the section on implicit IO in
`AsyncSession`, the walk below reached 146 chunks at depth 2 and 188 more at depth 4, so 335 of the
407 chunks lay within four hops. Without the hubs it reached 110.

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE edges (src, dst) AS (
    SELECT 'c' || chunk_id, 'e' || entity_id FROM doc_mentions
    UNION ALL
    SELECT 'e' || entity_id, 'c' || chunk_id FROM doc_mentions
),
walk (node, depth) AS (
    SELECT 'c201', 0
    UNION
    SELECT e.dst, w.depth + 1
    FROM walk w JOIN edges e ON e.src = w.node
    WHERE w.depth < 4
)
SELECT depth, count(*) AS new_nodes
FROM (SELECT node, min(depth) AS depth FROM walk GROUP BY node) first_seen
GROUP BY depth ORDER BY depth;
```

The condition on `depth` ends the walk, because the graph has cycles. `UNION` drops duplicate rows,
and the outer query counts each node at the depth where it first appears.

## Expansion from the nearest chunks

A retrieval step needs only two hops, from the seed chunks that vector search returned through their
entities to other chunks. The query below ranks each new chunk by the entities it shares with the
seeds, and weights each shared entity by its inverse document frequency, `ln(N / df)`, so that a link
through `Session` counts for little and a link through a rare name such as `AsyncSession.run_sync`
counts for a lot:

```sql
WITH seeds AS (SELECT unnest($1::int[]) AS id),
idf AS (
    SELECT entity_id, ln((SELECT count(*) FROM doc_chunks)::float / count(*)) AS w
    FROM doc_mentions GROUP BY entity_id
)
SELECT m2.chunk_id, sum(idf.w) AS score
FROM seeds
JOIN doc_mentions m1 ON m1.chunk_id = seeds.id
JOIN doc_mentions m2 ON m2.entity_id = m1.entity_id
JOIN idf ON idf.entity_id = m1.entity_id
WHERE m2.chunk_id NOT IN (SELECT id FROM seeds)
GROUP BY m2.chunk_id
ORDER BY score DESC
LIMIT 5;
```

The query took about 2 ms on top of the vector search, which took about the same.

## Retrieval compared

The notebook asks 14 questions about the documentation, many of which span two pages, such as lazy
loading in the query guide and implicit IO in the asyncio extension. Each question lists the sections
that answer it, chosen by hand, and recall is the share of those sections that at least one retrieved
chunk belongs to. Every method except the first returns ten chunks:

| method | mean recall | better than vector 10 | worse than vector 10 |
|---|---|---|---|
| vector 5 | 0.63 | 0 | 6 |
| vector 10 | 0.79 | | |
| vector 5 + graph 5, weighted by IDF | 0.72 | 1 | 4 |
| vector 5 + graph 5, unweighted | 0.71 | 1 | 4 |
| vector 5 + the 5 nearest two-hop neighbours | 0.79 | 1 | 1 |

Graph expansion raised recall from 0.63 to 0.72 over the five nearest chunks alone, but the next five
nearest chunks raised it to 0.79. The graph won one question, on `expire_on_commit`, where it brought
in the section on implicit IO in `AsyncSession` from another page, and lost four. Using the graph only
as a filter, by taking the nearest chunks among the seeds' two-hop neighbours, picked the same five
chunks as plain vector search on 9 of the 14 questions, because the hubs put most chunks within two
hops of any seed.

In this corpus the edges are API names, and the results suggest that chunks sharing API names are
already close in embedding space, so the graph mostly finds what similarity finds. A graph should add more where its
edges carry relations that similarity misses, such as facts about the same company spread over
documents that otherwise share few words, although the lab did not measure that case.

## A GraphRAG library

[postgres-graph-rag](https://github.com/h4gen/postgres-graph-rag) (0.1.2, MIT) packages the same
design for arbitrary text. It asks OpenAI or Gemini to extract entities and relations, stores them
with pgvector embeddings in one Postgres database, and expands a vector search with recursive CTEs.
Its README describes it as an early version whose interface can still change.
:::
